rationale: First assessed edition. The incumbent opened the case with an empty ledger, no featured set, no accounts and a null assessment; the ledger now carries 48 claims, 12 evidence records (all weak, all from the founder's single unverified page), 3 research items and 12 plates, so the judgment moves from none to a complete assessment and this edition returns one. No panel dissent is in the packet. QUESTION: kept (null) — the inputs have not moved it; the founding wording still contains every account treated. ACCOUNTS: supplied for the first time, in the founding pages' own terms (common source / lost civilisation, long-distance contact, convergence, later retelling), because the incumbent had none. FEATURED SET (24), chosen by stakes as the map of the controversy: the method hinge (C002) and the three governing mechanism claims (C026, C065, C036 is catalogued and spanned but not featured); the rung of each competing account — lost-civilisation (C035), retelling (C034), convergence for the hands (C047); every claim that has an evidence record (C005, C025, C056, C057, C027, C037, C038, C009, C015); and the decisive observation in each theme — bird-men (C004, C059), handled objects (C012, C044), navel (C018, C015), civilisers (C028, C053), floods (C031, C054). Fine-grained children stay catalogued under parents: C060–C064 under C059, C066 duplicates C012, C016 under C015, C021/C023/C046/C048/C049–C051 under C047, C055 under C031/C054, C043 under C044, C052 under C053, C058 under C059; C003, C010, C019, C045 are spanned or mentioned but carry low stakes for the thesis. CASE VERDICT: unresolved, justified rather than defaulted — the ledger holds one self-published source and no primary text, so the featured hypothesis has neither support nor refutation, while the little evidence present (high catalogue base rates, kind-matched controls changing lineup results, the lineup signal confounded by compressed accounts) leans toward convergence and retelling. The single record whose removal would most change the verdict is DEEP-E020: without it nothing in the ledger points toward a resemblance beyond base rates. CRUX ORDER: R003 leads because it tests the one positive signal directly; R002 next because it decides the navel theme; R001 replaces captions with primaries but is low-diagnostic for the thesis. ARTICLE: written as a first telling for a general reader, theme by theme, with the four accounts set side by side and what-would-change-our-mind visible; all twelve plates seated for the first time (none were seated in the incumbent).
accounts: The resemblances descend from one common source — at its strongest, a lost civilisation whose emissaries carried the images and stories outward
The resemblances record long-distance contact between particular cultures, with dated intermediates and a plausible route
The resemblances are independent inventions converging on the same forms from shared bodies, animals, materials and practical problems
The resemblances are largely made after the fact — by translation, borrowing, comparative writing and the selection of matching examples from a very large pool
article:
## The pattern people see

Set the pictures out in a row and the resemblance does its work before anyone has made an argument. An eagle-headed figure strides across a palace wall from Nimrud with a bucket in one hand and a cone in the other. A vulture spreads its wings on a Neolithic pillar at Göbekli Tepe, and along the pillar's top edge sit three arched shapes with handles. A seated man on an Olmec boulder from La Venta holds a small bag inside the coils of a crested serpent. Two bird-headed men face one another on the back of a statue taken from Rapa Nui. A netted stone at Delphi marks the navel of the world; so, in their own languages, do places in the Andes and the Pacific. A teacher comes from the sea, brings the arts, and leaves. A flood drowns everyone but a few.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P01}

The eye reads these as kin. The question this case asks is whether history does — and, just as much, how one could tell. The founder's Deep Memory pages put the question without answering it: how much of the resemblance belongs to a shared past, and how much to the ways people make images, tell stories and look for connections? Their working rule is that [the historical meaning of a visual resemblance depends on the objects' dates, contexts, differences and possible connections, not on the resemblance alone]{claim=DEEP-C002}. Everything below is an attempt to apply that rule to a ledger that is, so far, almost empty.

### How thin the ground is

A reader should know before going further what this case has to weigh. Every evidence record in the ledger comes from one source: the founder's own home page, a self-published web essay that describes itself as AI-assisted and reports five investigations its author ran. It is what the method calls a *self-report* — an author's statement of an unaudited result — and it is admitted as weak support at most. None of the primary literature the page leans on is yet in the ledger: not the wear-trace study of the Jiroft object, not the excavators' discussion of Pillar 43, not the published study of the Rapa Nui statue in the British Museum, not the fragments of Berossus. So nothing here is graded above “weakly supported”, and most of the claims that matter are graded “unresolved”: they stand in the catalogue, anchored to the page that made them, with no evidence record for or against. That is not a finding that they are false. It is a finding that they are untested, and a list of what would test them.

## Four accounts, set side by side

The founding pages name four explanations and insist that more than one can be true in different cases. This edition treats them as the live accounts.

- **A common source.** The forms and stories descend from one ancestor and were carried outward. In its strongest version — the lost-civilisation account — that ancestor is an unknown society of great age and capability whose emissaries taught the rest. It predicts that the specific composites (this pose with this object in this arrangement; this arrival, teaching and departure in this order) recur more often than chance across the compared cultures, and that the oldest examples cluster near the source.
- **Long-distance contact.** Particular cultures met and exchanged images or stories, with no single ancestor. It predicts dated intermediates and a plausible route, and resemblance strongest where the route runs.
- **Independent invention, or convergence.** Similar bodies, animals, materials and practical problems make similar forms; similar experiences of disaster make similar stories. It predicts that the broad classes are common everywhere, that a handle or a folded hand appears wherever carvers face the same problem, and that the specific composites do not travel together more than comparison bundles do.
- **Later retelling.** Much of the resemblance is made after the fact: by translation, by borrowing between cultures after contact, by comparative writers who smooth different stories into one biography, and by the selection of matching examples from a very large pool. It predicts that similarity grows between an original account and its modern summary, and that details associated with a famous version turn up unevenly, where that version was preached.

The rest of this article takes the themes in turn, asks what the ledger holds for each account, and names the observation that would decide between them.

## Bird-men

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P10}

The gallery of bird-headed figures runs from the Shaft Scene at Lascaux — a stick-figure man with a bird's head falling beside a wounded bison, a bird on a staff nearby — through Egyptian gods and Assyrian genii to costumed dancers in the Americas and the birdman cult of Rapa Nui. The founding pages themselves supply the first objection: [the description “bird-man” groups at least three distinct ideas — a deity with a bird's head, a person wearing feathers, and a person transforming into a bird]{claim=DEEP-C004}. If the compared images fall into different ones of these, the parallel is not one resemblance but three weaker ones. This edition grades that distinction as provisionally supported on priors — the gallery plainly spans all three — while noting that no evidence record has yet tested it.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P05}

The Rapa Nui example is where dates bite. Hoa Hakananai'a, the basalt moai taken from Orongo and now in the British Museum, carries on its back two facing birdmen, a ring and girdle, komari and paddles. The claim that matters most is that [the birdman carvings on the back were added later than the statue's manufacture]{claim=DEEP-C059}, itself placed at around 1000–1200 CE. If so, the Rapa Nui leg of the bird-man comparison is not only an ocean away from Lascaux and Nimrud but many thousands of years later than the one and two millennia later than the other — and centuries later than the statue it decorates. The ledger holds no evidence record for this: the published study of the statue is named in the research programme but has not been read. The claim is unresolved.

The catalogue experiment gives the other half of the picture. It reports that [a broad bird-person motif class occurs in 55% of 926 sampled traditions]{claim=DEEP-C005}. A *base rate* is the frequency of a thing in the population at large; a motif found in more than half of all sampled traditions is one you would expect to meet in any two cultures picked at random. That number, if it holds, is the single strongest reason in the ledger not to be surprised by a bird-man in two places. But the page qualifies its own figure twice, and the ledger records both qualifications: the catalogue's coverage is uneven, particularly for the ancient Near East and Rapa Nui — the very regions compared — and broad narrative categories are not the specific images or place names in the claim. A class that includes every winged soul and feathered dancer does not tell you how often a profile head, a bent limb and a rounded form nearby occur together. That composite, not the class, is the thing a common-source account needs, and no one has yet counted it.

## The handled objects

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P02}

Four objects make the comparison: the three arched forms on Pillar 43, the bucket carried by the Assyrian genii, the carved chlorite objects from the Halil Rud valley in Iran, and the small pouch held by the seated figure on Monument 19 at La Venta. Their outlines rhyme; the founding pages say so, and this edition agrees that they are worth looking at closely. Then the pages make the distinction the whole theme turns on: [shape and function are separate questions]{claim=DEEP-C065}.

The four are not on the same footing. For the Assyrian object, [ritual context supports a bucket-and-purifier interpretation]{claim=DEEP-C044}; the *banduddû* is [named in ritual texts]{claim=DEEP-C043}, and the cone in the genie's other hand is what sprinkles from it. For the Göbekli forms, [the function remains uncertain]{claim=DEEP-C012}: no secure identification has been published. The comparison, in other words, sets a known bucket beside three shapes whose purpose no one knows. If the Göbekli forms turned out to be containers, the resemblance would gain a rung; if they turned out to be something with no handle at all, it would lose one. Neither the Assyrian texts nor the excavators' discussion has been retrieved for this ledger, and both claims are unresolved.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P04}

The Jiroft object is the one case where function has been tested physically. The page reports that [the chlorite “handbag” in the National Museum of Iran shows wear on its handle consistent with having hung on a cord]{claim=DEEP-C009}, and points to a published wear-trace study for it. The ledger holds that pointer, not the study; the record is graded weakly supported, and its second reader would call it context rather than support. Retrieving the study is desk work, and it is in the research programme.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P03}

At La Venta, the figure's pouch is [usually read as an incense bag]{claim=DEEP-C010}, and the serpent that frames him is [often called the earliest known feathered serpent]{claim=DEEP-C003}. Neither reading has an evidence record yet.

What would move this theme? A handle is a practical solution that can recur wherever people carry things. What a common-source account needs, and what convergence does not predict, is that the *particular* handle — its attachment, its proportion to the body, its decoration, the figures beside it — recurs more often across the compared objects than across a control set of handled containers from cultures known to be unconnected. No one has run that comparison.

## Pigs, lizards and other stone animals

The animal comparisons extend the same logic. A low body, a raised back and a projecting snout make a boar legible across any distance; splayed limbs and open jaws make a crouching predator. Here the ledger holds one narrow observation: the Göbekli Tepe excavation team's discussion of Enclosure C [distinguishes boars from snarling predators]{claim=DEEP-C045} — that is, the people who dug the site read the animals in their setting, as an arrangement, not as isolated silhouettes. The founding pages are right that “lizard” should stay a proposed identification where the animal is uncertain, and that the next useful comparison is with other securely identified pig and boar sculptures rather than with whatever looks alike. Nothing in this theme is graded; it awaits objects with museum numbers.

## The navel of the world

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P06}

The linguistic parallel is the most evocative and, on inspection, the most fragile. Delphi's *omphalos* — the netted stone said to mark where Zeus's eagles met — is Greek and ancient. Cusco is glossed as the navel of the Inca world in Garcilaso's account, written after the conquest. Rapa Nui is Te Pito o te Henua, and a smooth stone near Ahu Te Pito Kura carries a name [glossed as “navel of light”]{claim=DEEP-C019}. Göbekli Tepe means “navel hill” in Turkish.

The founding pages' own claim is the crux: [these are different kinds of evidence, differing in language, date of first record and whether the ancient builders used the name]{claim=DEEP-C018}. This edition grades it provisionally supported on priors — Greek, Spanish, Rapanui and Turkish are four languages, recorded across some two and a half millennia — while noting that none of the four source histories has been retrieved. The sharpest test is the Turkish name. If [the modern Turkish name Göbekli Tepe describes the shape of the mound]{claim=DEEP-C015}, it is a descriptive toponym given long after the builders were gone and says nothing about what they believed. The page states exactly this, and adds that [the Kurdish names for the site mean “wish hill”]{claim=DEEP-C016}; but the ledger's one evidence record on the site's names covers the Kurdish gloss, not the Turkish, and neither is sourced on the page. The claim is unresolved, and the second item of the research order is to trace all four names to their first attestation.

What would change the picture: an early, builder-attested “navel” usage at two or more of the sites. What would settle it the other way: source histories showing, as the page proposes, that one name is a modern description, one a colonial gloss, and only Delphi's an ancient sacred designation in the language of the people who used it. A shared bodily metaphor for a centre is possible in any language; a particular inherited usage would need more than this.

## Hands on the belly

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P07}

The hands are part of what makes the monuments feel related. [Arms and hands are carved on the central T-pillars of Enclosure D at Göbekli Tepe]{claim=DEEP-C023}; the shaft is a body and the T a stylised head. Urfa Man, a life-size limestone statue from Şanlıurfa of about 9000 BCE with dark inlaid eyes, [holds its hands over the genitals]{claim=DEEP-C021}. The moai of Ahu Tongariki, carved some ten millennia later, meet their hands low on the abdomen above the belt. The Ponce monolith at Tiwanaku [holds its hands to the chest]{claim=DEEP-C050}, one of them around [a snuff tablet]{claim=DEEP-C051}.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P08}

The founding pages make the observation the eye tends to skip: a hand across the abdomen and a hand at the groin are close in outline but different observations. And they offer the convergence account in its plainest form. [Carving limbs against a stone body can protect them from breakage]{claim=DEEP-C046}, so [material constraints are a plausible contributor to the hands-on-body pose]{claim=DEEP-C047}. This edition grades that provisionally supported on priors: any carver of a monolith knows what happens to a free-standing arm. The pages are equally right that [material constraint as a contributor to the pose does not settle its symbolic meaning]{claim=DEEP-C048} — a constraint explains why hands rest against the body, not why they rest at the abdomen rather than the groin or the chest. The observation that would decide between constraint and descent is a survey of stone figures in the same media from cultures with no possible connection: if the pose varies with the stone and the tool, constraint wins; if it clusters along a route, something else is happening.

## Serpents, and the feathered serpent

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P12}

Snakes are everywhere in the gallery: coiled around the Olmec figure at La Venta, gripped by the hero on the Jiroft object, projecting in feathered collars from the Temple of the Feathered Serpent at Teotihuacan. The catalogue experiment reports [a broad cosmic-serpent motif class in 37% of sampled traditions]{claim=DEEP-C025} — another high base rate, graded weakly supported on the same self-reported footing as the bird-men figure. The feathered serpent of Mesoamerica is a much more specific thing than “snake”, and any comparison worth making has to preserve the feathers, the head, the body's arrangement and its relation to a human figure.

The page adds the methodological point that governs both catalogue results: [a catalogue's geographical distribution of a broad motif class cannot by itself distinguish independent invention from very old transmission]{claim=DEEP-C026}. The same map is compatible with a serpent invented a hundred times and a serpent inherited once. Distinguishing them takes dated intermediates or a model with stated assumptions — neither of which the ledger yet holds.

Taken together, the catalogue experiment's headline is the most consequential thing in the case and the least tested. It reports that [the three broad motif classes — birds, serpents, sacred centres — are each widespread]{claim=DEEP-C056}, and that [their bundle does not stand out against the study's documentation-preserving comparisons]{claim=DEEP-C057}. If the second holds, then finding birds, serpents and a sacred centre together in a tradition is no rarer than finding any comparable trio of common motifs — which is what convergence predicts and a common source does not. But the ledger contains no evidence record supporting that finding, only the page's two qualifications of it. It is graded unresolved, and it is the claim whose data this edition would most like to see.

## The people who brought the arts

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P09}

The narrative parallel is as arresting as the visual one. A figure arrives, often from the sea; teaches writing, agriculture, law or craft; changes human life; departs, sometimes promising to return. Oannes in Babylonia, Viracocha in the Andes, Quetzalcoatl in Mexico and Bochica among the Muisca recur in the comparison. The founding pages' caution is that the exact arrival, teaching and departure have to be read in each account, not supplied by a composite biography.

One of the figures has a dated image behind him. On a basalt basin from Assur, the god Ea stands with streams flowing from him beside a fish-cloaked sage; the page holds that [this fish-cloaked figure is the apkallu type the texts actually name]{claim=DEEP-C052}, and that [Berossus's Oannes corresponds to it]{claim=DEEP-C053}. Oannes is thus the one civiliser with a documented iconographic type — but Berossus survives only in later excerpts, and neither the excerpts nor the apkallu texts have been read for this ledger. Unresolved.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P11}

At Tiwanaku, the staff-bearing figure with the rayed head in the central register of the Gate of the Sun is often called Viracocha. The page's claim is that [that identification is a modern one]{claim=DEEP-C028}. If so, the most-reproduced “image of Viracocha” is not evidence that the story existed before the Spanish wrote it down. Unresolved, for want of a record.

The one measured result in this theme is the founder's V1 lineup experiment. AI judges were shown a civiliser account and asked to pick its partner from a lineup; [the claimed partner ranked first in 62.5% of completed lineups, against 9% for random pairs]{claim=DEEP-C027}. That is a real signal under the experiment's conditions, and the only evidence record in the ledger that points toward a resemblance beyond base rates. It is also, on the page's own statement, badly confounded: the lineups were recognisable, and they used compressed modern accounts. A model that has read the comparative literature knows that Viracocha and Quetzalcoatl are supposed to match. And a lineup of modern summaries measures the similarity of modern summaries. That is exactly the mechanism the retelling account proposes — [stories can become more alike than their originals through translation, borrowing and comparative writing]{claim=DEEP-C034} — and the page's later audit of the original passages has not rerun the test. The decisive experiment leads this edition's research order: rerun the lineup with human raters on unrecognisable passages from the original sources — Berossus via his excerptors, the early Andean chroniclers, Sahagún, Simón — against random hero narratives, and see whether 62.5% survives.

The lost-civilisation account attaches to these figures its strongest claims: that the teachers were emissaries of a real, identifiable, technically advanced society of great age. The page's answer, which this edition adopts on priors, is that [similarity between motifs alone cannot establish a lost-civilisation account's claims about the source's identity, date and capabilities]{claim=DEEP-C035}. A resemblance can at most suggest a connection; who was connected to whom, when, and what they could do, needs evidence of a different kind, and none is in this ledger.

## What survives the water

Flood stories raise several questions at once: whether people remember local disasters, whether particular stories travelled, and whether traditions preserve much older environmental knowledge. The founder's text-coding pilot had an AI code the details of 263 flood-story summaries. It reports that [the coded details cluster by region]{claim=DEEP-C031}, that [details associated with Genesis are unevenly distributed]{claim=DEEP-C054}, and that [generic flood motifs are widespread]{claim=DEEP-C055}.

Each of the four accounts can live with regional clustering: inheritance with regional drift, contact along routes, independent memory of local floods, retelling in regional missions. The uneven distribution of Genesis details is the more pointed finding, because it is what the retelling account predicts — and yet, as the page says, recording a story after contact does not establish that it was borrowed. None of these three claims has an evidence record in the ledger, and the pilot itself coded one compiler's summaries rather than a representative collection of original accounts. All three are unresolved. What would move them: the coded data released and re-coded by human readers against original texts, with the Genesis-associated details dated, where possible, to before or after missionary contact.

## Indus and rongorongo

The companion project compares the sign inventories of two undeciphered scripts and the illustrations used to connect them. Its governing claim is the one this case would apply everywhere: [a visual resemblance between signs of two undeciphered scripts does not establish shared sound, meaning or descent]{claim=DEEP-C036}. Sign shapes converge between scripts known to be unrelated; the ledger holds the principle and none of the companion's results.

## When resemblance becomes evidence

Can the resemblance people see be measured at all? The founder's three image pilots tried to make AI judges rank objects by likeness. The page reports that [judges disagreed strongly with one another about the same objects]{claim=DEEP-C037}, and that [matching the kinds of objects in a lineup changed the lineup result]{claim=DEEP-C038}. The second has an evidence record and is graded weakly supported; the first does not, and is unresolved.

The second finding is the more important. *Diagnosticity* is how much an observation decides between rival explanations. If a lineup that pits a pillar against a moai, a relief and a boulder ranks them one way, and a lineup of pillars against pillars ranks them another, then part of the original resemblance was an artefact of comparing unlike kinds — and that is a finding about every side-by-side gallery, including the one that opens this article.

## Where this leaves the question

The ledger, read strictly, says this. The broad classes — bird-people, cosmic serpents, sacred centres — are common enough that meeting them in two cultures is expected. Whether the specific composites are rarer than chance has not been counted. The one positive signal, the civiliser lineup, is confounded in exactly the way the retelling account predicts. The navel parallel rests on four names whose source histories have not been traced, one of them very probably modern. The dating that would place the Rapa Nui birdmen centuries after their statue, and the function that would make one “handbag” a known bucket, are asserted but unrecorded.

The verdict of this edition is *unresolved*, and the word is chosen, not defaulted to. It means the featured hypothesis — that the resemblances record a shared past — has neither support nor refutation in the ledger, because the ledger holds one unverified source and no primary text. It does not mean the evidence is balanced. Such evidence as there is leans, weakly and by the founder's own report, toward base rates, convergence and retelling.

What would change our mind, in either direction:

- A blind human lineup of original civiliser passages that beats random pairs by a margin like V1's — or one that does not.
- A count of specific composites (pose plus object plus arrangement; handle attachment plus proportion plus decoration) across the compared objects and a kind-matched control set.
- The four navel names traced to first attestation, with the builders' usage documented or shown absent.
- The excavators' discussion of Pillar 43, the wear-trace study of the Jiroft object and the published study of Hoa Hakananai'a read, and their statements recorded in place of the page's captions.
- Dated intermediates and a route for any one of the parallels.

The best argument for the shared past that this edition does not answer is that the null result of the catalogue experiment, by the page's own admission, tests broad classes rather than the specific images in the claim — so the strongest evidence against a common source has not actually been aimed at it — and that the lineup signal, however confounded, is a measurement, where the critics have so far offered only reasons. Both are fair. Both point to the same thing: the next steps are small, cheap and named, and this case waits on them.

assessment.synthesis: The ledger holds twelve evidence records, all weak, all from one source: the founder's self-published, AI-assisted home page reporting its own unaudited experiments. No primary text — excavation report, wear study, statue study, chronicle, ritual text — has been retrieved. On that footing the featured hypothesis (that the resemblances record a shared past) can be neither supported nor refuted, and the verdict is unresolved. The word is chosen, not defaulted to: the alternative verdicts each require a record the ledger lacks. Such evidence as exists leans toward the conventional accounts. The catalogue experiment reports base rates of 55% (bird-person) and 37% (cosmic serpent) for broad classes, which make a bird-man or a serpent in two cultures expected rather than surprising (DEEP-E013, E016), though the page's own qualifiers (E018, E019) note uneven coverage and that broad classes are not the specific images. Its headline null — the motif bundle does not stand out against comparison bundles (C057) — has no supporting record at all. The only record pointing toward resemblance beyond base rates is the V1 civiliser lineup (E020, E021: 62.5% vs 9%), which the page itself confounds with recognisable, compressed modern accounts — exactly the retelling mechanism (C034). The image pilots' one recorded finding (E022) is that kind-matched controls change lineup results, a warning about every side-by-side gallery. The single evidence record whose removal would most change the case verdict is DEEP-E020: without it nothing in the ledger points toward a resemblance beyond base rates, and the case would tilt from unresolved toward weakly supported for convergence and retelling.
assessment.steelman: The strongest case for a shared past that this assessment does not answer has two parts. First, the only evidence in the ledger that could count against a common source — the catalogue experiment's finding that the motif bundle does not stand out — tests broad narrative classes, and the page concedes (E019) that broad classes are not the specific images or place names in the claim. A composite of profile head, bent limb and rounded form, or of handle attachment, proportion and decoration, has never been counted against a control set; so the null result has not actually been aimed at the hypothesis it is taken to undermine. Second, the V1 lineup produced a measured signal (62.5% first-rank against 9% for random pairs) under stated conditions, and the objections to it — recognisability, compression — are reasons, not measurements; until the blind human rerun is done, the one experiment in the ledger with a result favours the resemblance being real. Neither point changes a verdict, because neither adds a record; both name the test that would.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: That a set of recurring forms and stories — bird-headed figures, small handled objects, hands folded on the body of a stone figure, sacred centres named as a navel, feathered serpents, teachers who arrive, bring the arts and depart, floods that few survive — appear across distant ancient cultures (Göbekli Tepe, Nimrud, Jiroft, La Venta, Delphi, Cusco, Tiwanaku, Rapa Nui) because they descend from a shared past, whether one common source or long-distance contact, rather than arising independently or being assembled after the fact by retelling and comparison.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not in whether the outlines rhyme — everyone agrees they do — but in four places. Whether the broad classes' high base rates dispose of the parallels, or whether the specific composites are rarer than chance (no count exists). Whether the civiliser lineup signal measures the original accounts or the modern summaries that compress them. Whether the four navel names share anything beyond a bodily metaphor, given their different languages, dates and users. And whether resemblance can be measured at all when kind-matched controls change the ranking and AI judges disagree.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: For the shared-past account: dated intermediates and a plausible route for any one parallel; a specific composite (pose plus object plus arrangement; handle attachment plus proportion plus decoration) occurring across the compared objects more often than across a kind-matched control set from unconnected cultures; a blind human lineup of original civiliser passages that beats random pairs by a margin like V1's; an early, builder-attested navel usage at two or more sites. Against it: the catalogue's bundle comparison data released and holding under narrower classes; the blind rerun collapsing toward chance; source histories showing the Göbekli name modern and descriptive, the Cusco gloss colonial, the Viracocha identification modern; the Rapa Nui birdmen dated centuries after their statue; the Göbekli handled forms identified as something other than containers.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Broad motif classes are common everywhere — a bird-person in more than half of sampled traditions, a cosmic serpent in more than a third — so meeting them in two cultures is the expectation, not the anomaly. Shared bodies, animals, materials and practical problems produce convergent forms: a handle is how anyone carries a thing, hands against a stone body are how a monolith keeps its arms. The compared set is selected for resemblance from a very large pool of objects, and comparing unlike kinds inflates the likeness that kind-matched controls remove. Stories converge through translation, comparative writing and missionary contact, so compressed modern summaries of Oannes, Viracocha and Quetzalcoatl are more alike than their originals. The navel names are four languages recorded across two and a half millennia, one of them a modern Turkish description of a mound's shape.

components.label: The visual parallels: bird-men, handled objects, hands, serpents
components.note: The outlines rhyme, but every rung that would make the rhyme historical — the later date of the Rapa Nui birdmen (C059), the unknown function of the Göbekli forms (C012), the textual function of the banduddû (C044), the Jiroft wear (C009) — is asserted on the founder's page without a primary record. Material constraint (C047) is a plausible convergence account for the hands, on priors.

components.label: The catalogue base rates and the bundle test
components.note: Self-reported base rates of 55% and 37% for broad classes (E013, E016) are the strongest reason in the ledger to expect these motifs anywhere; the page's own qualifiers (E018, E019) limit their reach, and the decisive null — the bundle does not stand out (C057) — has no supporting record.

components.label: The navel names
components.note: Four names in four languages recorded across millennia (C018, provisionally supported on priors); the Turkish name's modern descriptive origin (C015) has no record on the Turkish gloss, and none of the four source histories has been traced (R002).

components.label: The civiliser figures
components.note: The V1 lineup signal (62.5% vs 9%, E020/E021) is real under its conditions and the only positive record in the ledger; the page itself names the confounds — recognisable lineups, compressed modern accounts — that the retelling account predicts (C034). The Oannes–apkallu link (C053) and the modernity of the Viracocha identification (C028) are unrecorded.

components.label: The flood stories
components.note: Regional clustering and uneven Genesis-associated details (C031, C054) are what the pilot reports, but its record failed verification and the pilot coded one compiler's summaries by one AI; no evidence record stands.

components.label: Measuring the resemblance people see
components.note: That kind-matched controls change lineup results (C038) is weakly supported by E022 and is a warning about every side-by-side gallery; the reported inter-judge disagreement (C037) has no record. Neither pilot has been shown to reproduce human judgments of resemblance.

researchPriority.reason: The entire ledger rests on one unverified self-published source. Three desk-tier retrievals (the Pillar 43 discussion, the Jiroft wear study, the Hoa Hakananai'a study; the four navel-name source histories) would decide most featured observation claims one way or the other at near-zero cost, and the blind human lineup of original civiliser passages is a designed, small-grant test of the one positive signal in the case. The information gain per unit effort is unusually large.

claimAssessments.reasoning: A methodological principle rather than an empirical finding; the ledger holds no evidence record for or against it, and this grade rests on stated priors: no comparative discipline assigns a historical explanation to a resemblance without dates, contexts and differences. Anchored to the founder's page, which states it as its working rule.

treatment.plainLanguage: Two things looking alike tells you nothing about history until you know when and where each was made, how they differ, and whether their makers could have met.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Does not decide the thesis against any alternative; it governs how every other claim in the case is allowed to count. Its truth is what makes the base-rate and control results relevant.
treatment.strongestObjection: A sufficiently specific composite of features, measured against a control set, is itself evidence; the phrase 'not on the resemblance alone' understates what a well-controlled resemblance can show before any context is added.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A documented series of cases in which unaided visual resemblance correctly predicted a historical connection later confirmed by independent evidence, at a rate clearly better than chance.
A published method by which resemblance alone, without dates or contexts, discriminates transmission from convergence under stated assumptions.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The page reports that the bundle of three broad classes does not stand out against its documentation-preserving comparisons, but the ledger holds no evidence record supporting this — only the page's two qualifiers (E018, E019) on coverage and on the gap between broad classes and specific images. The comparison data have not been seen.

treatment.plainLanguage: Finding birds, serpents and a sacred centre together in one tradition is, by the founder's own experiment, no rarer than finding any comparable trio of common motifs together.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If true, the co-occurrence of the three classes is what chance and convergence predict and a common source does not; it is the most direct test in the ledger of whether the motif bundle is special. Its diagnosticity is capped by the coarseness of the classes tested.
treatment.strongestObjection: Broad narrative categories are not the specific images or place names in the claim, as the page itself says; a null on coarse classes could hide a real signal at the level of specific composites.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The experiment's comparison data released and reproducing the null.
A rerun with narrower classes (specific pose, object and arrangement) in which the bundle does stand out — or does not.
An independent catalogue with better coverage of the ancient Near East and Rapa Nui giving a different result.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Two weak self-report records (E020, E021) state the 62.5% and 9% figures as the page's own result. Run data are not retrieved; 'completed lineups' implies incomplete runs the page does not enumerate. The page's own limitations — recognisable lineups, compressed modern accounts — are recorded in the ledger only through the rejected record's reason, not as evidence.

treatment.plainLanguage: When AI judges were shown one civiliser story and asked to pick its partner from a lineup, they picked the claimed partner first about five times out of eight, against about one in eleven for random pairs.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The only record in the ledger pointing toward resemblance beyond base rates, but it cannot distinguish similarity of the original accounts from similarity manufactured by compressed modern retellings and by the judges' familiarity with the comparative literature — which is what the retelling account predicts.
treatment.strongestObjection: The lineups were recognisable: a model that has read the comparative literature knows Viracocha is supposed to match Quetzalcoatl, and a lineup of modern summaries measures the similarity of modern summaries.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A blind human rerun on unrecognisable passages from original sources (R003) that reproduces a margin like 62.5% vs 9%.
The same rerun collapsing toward chance, which would locate the signal in the retellings.
The V1 run data released and audited for incomplete runs and repeated items.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record in the ledger; graded on stated priors — documented cases of convergence through translation and comparative writing are well known in the study of myth, but none has been retrieved here. The page proposes it as one of its explanations, and its own V1 limitation (compressed accounts) is an instance of the mechanism.

treatment.plainLanguage: Stories can grow more alike than they started, because translators, borrowers and comparative writers smooth different accounts toward one another.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the retelling account's mechanism. If documented for the civiliser and flood stories, it dissolves the narrative parallels without any shared past; if the original passages are as alike as their summaries, it fails for those cases.
treatment.strongestObjection: Convergence in retelling does not preclude similarity in the originals; showing that summaries are more alike than sources does not show the sources are unalike.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Original passages (Berossus via excerptors, the Andean chroniclers, Sahagún, Simón) shown to share the specific sequence — sea arrival, particular crafts, catastrophe, departure with return promise — before any comparative writing.
Documented retellings showing no convergence relative to earlier attested versions.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record; graded on priors as a near-analytic point — a resemblance between motifs carries no information about a source's identity, date or capabilities, which are claims of a different kind. The page states it as its answer to the lost-civilisation account.

treatment.plainLanguage: Even if two images or stories really were connected, that alone cannot tell you who the connecting people were, when they lived, or what they could build.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Decides the lost-civilisation version of the common-source account against the ledger as it stands: nothing in it bears on identity, date or capability, so that account has no purchase here whatever the resemblances show.
treatment.strongestObjection: Proponents claim to offer more than similarity — geological, astronomical or genetic evidence — so the claim answers only the resemblance argument, not the account as its advocates state it.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Evidence of a specific kind — dated artefacts, texts or genetic signals — linking two of the compared cultures to an identifiable third source, entered into the ledger.
A demonstration that a specific composite of motifs can be dated or attributed from its form alone.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record; graded on priors — a present-day distribution map is compatible with many histories unless a model with stated assumptions is applied. The page states it as the scope note for its catalogue result.

treatment.plainLanguage: Knowing where a broad kind of story is found today does not tell you whether it was invented many times or inherited once.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Governs how the catalogue results count rather than deciding the thesis: it caps what the 55%, 37% and bundle findings can show about transmission versus convergence.
treatment.strongestObjection: Phylogenetic and areal models of motif distribution claim to discriminate inheritance from diffusion and invention under stated assumptions; the claim is true only 'by itself' and false once such a model is supplied.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A published model applied to the same catalogue that discriminates the histories with stated assumptions and reported uncertainty.
Dated intermediates for any motif, which would take the question out of distribution alone.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Two of the three classes have weak self-report records (E013 for bird-person at 55%, E016 for cosmic serpent at 37%); the third, sacred centres, has no figure recorded. The qualifiers E018 and E019 limit coverage and category reach.

treatment.plainLanguage: Birds, serpents and sacred centres, as broad story types, turn up in a large share of the world's recorded traditions.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Establishes the base rate against which every pairwise parallel must be judged: high base rates make individual matches expected. It does not touch the specific composites.
treatment.strongestObjection: The catalogue's coverage is uneven for the ancient Near East and Rapa Nui, and the sacred-centre class was never quantified on the page.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The coded data reproducing all three frequencies, including sacred centres.
An independent catalogue giving markedly lower frequencies for the compared regions.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Weak self-report records E013 and E014 state the 55% of 926 figure; E015's direction is disputed by its second reader as a scope limitation rather than support. E018 and E019 qualify: uneven coverage, and broad classes are not the specific images.

treatment.plainLanguage: More than half of the 926 traditions sampled have some kind of bird-person in their stories.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A base rate above one half makes a bird-man in any two cultures the expectation, undercutting the surprise on which the parallel trades; it says nothing about how often a profile head, bent limb and rounded form occur together.
treatment.strongestObjection: A class that includes every winged soul and feathered dancer is far broader than the compared images, and the catalogue underrepresents exactly the regions compared.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The experiment's coded data reproducing the proportion.
A count of the specific relational composite across a control set, showing it far rarer than the class.
An independent catalogue giving a substantially different frequency.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Weak self-report record E016 states the 37% figure; E017 is a scope caveat whose 'supports' direction its second reader disputes. E018 and E019 qualify coverage and category reach.

treatment.plainLanguage: About a third of the sampled traditions have a cosmic serpent of some kind.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Sets the base rate for serpents generally; the feathered serpent is a far more specific composite that the class does not measure.
treatment.strongestObjection: The class is broad and the catalogue's coverage uneven; a cosmic serpent and a feathered serpent framing a seated man are not the same observation.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The coded data reproducing the proportion.
A count of the feathered-serpent composite specifically across a control set.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record; graded on priors — the gallery the page assembles plainly spans a bird-headed deity, a person in feathered costume and a soul-bird or transforming figure, and these are distinct ideas in the traditions that hold them. Whether the specifically compared images fall into different categories has not been tested.

treatment.plainLanguage: 'Bird-man' is not one thing: a god with a bird's head, a dancer in feathers and a person turning into a bird are three different ideas.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If the compared bird-men belong to different categories, one strong parallel becomes three weak ones, which favours convergence; if they share a category and a composite, the parallel survives the distinction.
treatment.strongestObjection: The three ideas might descend from one older idea, so dividing them assumes what is at issue.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Each compared image assigned to a category from its own culture's texts or contexts, showing whether they match.
A demonstration that the three ideas are historically linked in some documented tradition.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record. The page's caption states the carvings are later than the statue; the published study of Hoa Hakananai'a that would settle it is named in the research programme but not retrieved.

treatment.plainLanguage: The two birdmen on the back of the Easter Island statue in the British Museum were carved some time after the statue itself was made.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If true, the Rapa Nui leg of the bird-man parallel is centuries later than its statue and millennia later than the Old World examples, which makes any common source improbably remote; if the carvings were original, the gap narrows only slightly.
treatment.strongestObjection: Late carvings can carry old ideas; the date of the relief is not the date of the birdman concept on the island.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The published study (Pitts et al. 2014) retrieved and read for its dating of the reliefs relative to the statue.
Independent dating of birdman imagery elsewhere on Rapa Nui.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record; graded on priors as a conceptual distinction the page states and archaeology observes: an object's outline and its use are established by different evidence.

treatment.plainLanguage: That two objects have the same outline is one question; what each was for is another.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Governs the handled-object theme rather than deciding it: it separates the known bucket from the unknown forms and prevents the outline alone from carrying the parallel.
treatment.strongestObjection: Inferring function from shared shape is what archaeology does daily; the distinction, pressed too hard, would forbid ordinary typology.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The Göbekli forms given a secure functional identification that matches or contradicts the Assyrian bucket.
Wear or residue evidence on the compared objects showing convergent use.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record. The page and the plate record state the banduddû is a bucket named in ritual texts and paired with a sprinkling cone; the texts have not been retrieved for this ledger. Priors favour it, but no record carries it.

treatment.plainLanguage: In Assyria the object the genie carries is a bucket used with a cone for ritual sprinkling — we know because the texts say so.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If true, the 'handbag' comparison sets a documented ritual bucket beside objects of unknown function, which weakens the parallel unless the others prove to be containers too.
treatment.strongestObjection: A functional reading in one culture does not exclude a shared symbolic meaning carried by the shape in others.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The ritual texts naming the banduddû and the cone retrieved and recorded.
Evidence that the Göbekli or La Venta objects were containers of the same kind.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record. The page and the plate record state the function is unknown; the excavation team's Pillar 43 discussion, which would show whether any functional identification has been published, is not retrieved.

treatment.plainLanguage: Nobody has securely established what the three handled shapes on Pillar 43 were.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Leaves the Göbekli end of the handled-object parallel uncontrolled: a container reading would strengthen the parallel, a reading as buildings or something else would end it.
treatment.strongestObjection: The absence of a functional identification is itself informative in neither direction; it only shows the comparison is between a known and an unknown.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Notroff et al. retrieved and read for the excavators' own statement on the forms.
A published functional identification of the forms by the excavation team.

claimAssessments.reasoning: One weak record (E023) — the page's pointer to the Vidale & Micheli wear-trace study — whose second reader would call it context rather than support, since the study itself has not been retrieved.

treatment.plainLanguage: The stone 'handbag' from Jiroft is worn on its handle in the way a thing gets worn when it hangs on a cord.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Establishes a practical function for one object, which fits convergence (handles are for hanging) but says little about the other three objects or about any connection.
treatment.strongestObjection: The record is a caption's paraphrase of an unretrieved paper; the wear reading is the study's, not the ledger's.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The wear-trace study retrieved and its findings recorded (R001).
Comparable wear analysis on the other handled objects.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record; graded on priors — the four names are in Greek, Spanish gloss of Quechua, Rapanui and Turkish, first recorded across roughly two and a half millennia, and at least one (the Turkish) postdates its builders by millennia. None of the source histories has been retrieved (R002).

treatment.plainLanguage: The four 'navel' names are not the same kind of evidence: they come from different languages, were written down at very different times, and in some cases were never used by the people who built the sites.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The rung on which the navel parallel stands or falls: if the names differ as proposed, the parallel reduces to a shared bodily metaphor; if two or more share an early, builder-attested usage, that is unexpected and would count for transmission.
treatment.strongestObjection: Differing source histories do not exclude an older shared metaphor beneath them; the claim shows the evidence is uneven, not that the idea is unconnected.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The four names traced to first attestation with the builders' usage documented or shown absent.
An early navel usage at two or more sites in the builders' own languages.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The only record on the site's names (E024) covers the Kurdish 'wish hill' gloss and, as its second reader notes, says nothing about the Turkish name's descriptive origin; the page gives no source for either etymology.

treatment.plainLanguage: 'Göbekli Tepe' is modern Turkish for a hill shaped like a navel — a description of the mound, not a sacred title.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If true, one of the four legs of the navel parallel is not ancient evidence at all, and the most-cited modern coincidence dissolves; if the name carried an older sacred sense, the parallel gains a leg.
treatment.strongestObjection: A descriptive toponym can inherit an older usage; showing the name is descriptive does not show it is unrelated to a sacred designation.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A Turkish or Kurdish toponymic record, or the excavation reports, dating and explaining the name (R002).
Evidence of a pre-modern sacred designation for the mound.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record; graded on priors — carving limbs against the body protects them, as any monolith carver knows, so constraint plausibly contributes to the pose. The claim is modest ('a plausible contributor'), and the page states it as one explanation among others.

treatment.plainLanguage: Stone arms break off; carving hands flat against the body is a practical way to keep them, so the shared pose may owe something to the stone.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The convergence account for the hands: if the pose varies with medium and tool across unconnected cultures, constraint explains it and descent is unneeded; it does not explain the specific position — abdomen, groin or chest.
treatment.strongestObjection: Constraint explains hands against the body, not hands at the abdomen rather than the groin or chest, and the founding pages themselves note that material constraint does not settle symbolic meaning.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A survey of stone figures in comparable media from unconnected cultures showing the pose tracks material and tool.
The same survey showing the specific hand position clusters along a plausible route regardless of medium.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record. The page and the plate record link Berossus's Oannes to the fish-cloaked apkallu type; Berossus survives only through later excerptors, and neither the fragments nor the apkallu texts have been retrieved.

treatment.plainLanguage: The fish-man Oannes whom Berossus describes as teaching the Babylonians is the same kind of figure as the fish-cloaked sages shown in Assyrian art.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Anchors one civiliser in a dated iconographic type and a named textual tradition — the one case where a civiliser story has a documented ancient source rather than a colonial or modern one — which is what a fair lineup would need as its control.
treatment.strongestObjection: Berossus is known only through Polyhistor and Eusebius; the correspondence may be tighter in the excerpts than in the original.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The Berossus fragments read against the apkallu texts and recorded.
Assyriological literature retrieved that names the fish-cloaked figures as apkallu.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record. The page and the plate record state the identification of the Gate of the Sun's staff-bearer as Viracocha is modern; no pre-modern naming has been sought in the ledger.

treatment.plainLanguage: Calling the central figure on Tiwanaku's Gate of the Sun 'Viracocha' is a modern habit, not something any ancient or early colonial source says.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If true, the most reproduced image of the Andean civiliser is not evidence that the story predates the Spanish chronicles, which removes a visual anchor from the civiliser parallel.
treatment.strongestObjection: The absence of a pre-modern name does not show the figure was not a creator deity, only that we do not know what it was called.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A pre-conquest or early colonial source naming the figure.
Archaeological literature on Tiwanaku iconography retrieved and read for the history of the identification.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record: the pilot's report was rejected on a locator mismatch. The pilot itself had one AI code a compiler's summaries of 263 stories rather than a representative collection of original accounts.

treatment.plainLanguage: Flood stories from the same part of the world tend to share details with each other more than with stories from elsewhere.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Regional structure is compatible with every account — inheritance with drift, contact along routes, local disaster memory, regional missions — so it decides little by itself; it becomes diagnostic only when specific details are dated.
treatment.strongestObjection: Clustering in a compiler's summaries coded by one AI may reflect the compiler and the coder more than the stories.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The coded data released and re-coded by human readers against original texts.
The pilot repeated on a representative collection of original accounts.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record, for the same reason as C031. The page states the finding and immediately cautions that recording after contact does not establish borrowing.

treatment.plainLanguage: Details that echo the Genesis flood — the raven and the dove, the ark, the rainbow — show up in some regions' stories much more than in others.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Uneven distribution of Genesis-associated details is what the retelling and contact accounts predict for stories recorded by missionaries; if the details were dated to before contact, it would instead favour inheritance. Its diagnosticity depends on dating the details, which the pilot did not do.
treatment.strongestObjection: Recording after contact does not establish borrowing; a detail can be both Genesis-like and native.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Genesis-associated details dated to before missionary contact in the regions where they cluster.
The coded data released and the coding reproduced by human readers.

claimAssessments.reasoning: One weak self-report record (E022) states that matching the kinds of objects changed the lineup result; pilot data are not retrieved and the page notes incomplete runs and cropping constrain the conclusions.

treatment.plainLanguage: When the AI judges compared like with like — pillars with pillars, statues with statues — the ranking of which objects looked most alike came out differently.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If controlling for kind changes the ranking, part of the resemblance in the original side-by-side galleries is an artefact of comparing unlike kinds — a finding about the method that generated the case's phenomenology.
treatment.strongestObjection: A single self-reported pilot with incomplete runs; AI judges have not been shown to reproduce human judgments of resemblance.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The pilot data released showing the kind-matched ranking.
A human-rater replication of the kind-matched lineup.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record bears on it: E022 concerns kind-matching, and its second reader notes it says nothing about inter-judge agreement. The page states strong disagreement between judges without statistics in the ledger.

treatment.plainLanguage: Different AI judges looking at the same two objects often disagreed sharply about how alike they were.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If the judges cannot agree, the resemblance people see has not yet been measured, and any lineup result — including the civiliser signal — inherits that uncertainty.
treatment.strongestObjection: Disagreement among models says nothing about whether humans agree; the finding is about the instrument, not the objects.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The pilots' inter-judge agreement statistics published.
A human-rater study of the same pairs showing whether people agree where the models did not.
